question: Recent media reports have highlighted concerns regarding AI-enabled smart glasses and other wearable devices capable of surreptitiously recording images and audio in public spaces. Particular concerns have been raised by women who report being unknowingly filmed and whose images may subsequently be shared online.

The rapid development of wearable devices combining cameras, microphones and AI raises important questions regarding privacy, data protection, transparency and public safety. While current EU legislation, specifically the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act, provides safeguards, the practical application of these rules to consumer AI wearables may require further clarification. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of AI-enabled smart glasses and similar wearable devices with current EU data protection, privacy and consumer protection legislation?

How is the Commission assessing the impact of such technologies on women, including risks related to gender-based harassment, non-consensual recording and the online dissemination of images, as well as the impact on women’s sense of safety and participation in public spaces?

Does the Commission intend, in cooperation with the European Data Protection Board and other relevant authorities, to issue guidance on the use of AI-enabled wearable devices and the processing of personal data collected from non-users?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1 requires that personal data processing is fair, transparent and lawful2 and in line with data protection by design and by default3.

Smart glasses are not a new technology, and the data protection authorities have previously examined their compliance with the GDPR and recommended measures to increase transparency towards individuals4. The impact on privacy and data protection of individuals is also discussed by the European Data Protection Board5.

In addition to data protection requirements, these products must fully comply with EU product safety legislation6. Depending on their primary function, they may also fall under sectoral rules. The use of such technologies may also raise concerns about technology-facilitated genderbased violence (TF-GBV).

Such concerns should be considered when applying the existing legal framework, including Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence (VAW Directive)7 which requires the criminalisation of the most widespread forms of TF-GBV by 14 June 2027.

The covert use of AI-enabled wearable devices to record and subsequently disseminate images online may fall within the scope of the VAW Directive’s framework. The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20308 also reaffirms the Commission’s commitment to preventing and combating all forms of violence against women, including TF-GBV.

This includes addressing emerging digital and AI-enabled risks that may disproportionately affect women and girls. Member State competent authorities and courts have a primary responsibility to monitor the application of the relevant legal provisions and to take the necessary steps for enforcement, without prejudice to the competences of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties.
